screens.title: Data Governance and Compliance in Azure Databases
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we examine how governance and compliance shape safe database operations in Azure. You will learn why classifying sensitive columns, auditing access, and choosing the right protection — masking versus client-side encryption — are foundational for meeting rules like GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI. We'll use the built-in tools Azure provides: Data Discovery & Classification, auditing to storage or Log Analytics, Dynamic Data Masking, and Always Encrypted. I will show practical examples you can run in a lab: a sample Customers table, how to mark columns as Confidential or Highly Confidential, and how to mask and test access for a non-privileged user. You will also see how PostgreSQL and MySQL handle auditing differently and when to stream logs for centralized analysis. By the end you should be able to decide when to mask, when to encrypt on the client, and how Azure Policy and Microsoft Defender for Cloud help you enforce and monitor those choices. Think about a dataset you manage: which columns should be classified and which feature protects them best?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Data Governance and Compliance

Learn to discover sensitive data, record activity, and apply masking or client-side encryption so that regulatory and business requirements are met without disrupting applications.

In this lesson
Practical steps to classify data, configure auditing across SQL, PostgreSQL and MySQL, apply Dynamic Data Masking, and design Always Encrypted deployments.
Why it matters
Regulations require evidence of protection and access control. Proper governance limits exposure and simplifies audits.
Explore Key Topics
Classification, Auditing, Masking, and Client-side Encryption in Azure SQL and managed databases.
Governance Snapshot
Classification feeds masking and auditing. Encryption protects highly sensitive columns from privileged users.
Classification
Data Discovery & Classification recommends labels like Confidential and Highly Confidential.
Auditing
Stream logs to storage, Log Analytics, or Event Hub for retention and analysis.
Protection
Use DDM for simple masking and Always Encrypted for client-side protection of sensitive columns.
Coming up
Hands-on demo: classify, mask, and test data access in a sample database.
Duration: ~10 minutes

screens.title: Why data governance and compliance matter
screens.narratorSegment: Data governance is the set of processes and responsibilities that ensure data is available, accurate, and secure. Compliance means meeting laws and regulations that control how personal or sensitive data is handled. In cloud databases, lack of governance can mean uncontrolled access, inconsistent protections, and failed audits — all of which create legal and business risk. For example, a retail application that stores credit card numbers without classification may expose financial data to developers, auditors, or third-party services unintentionally. Regulations such as GDPR or PCI require not only technical controls but also evidence: classification reports, audit logs, and retention policies. A common misconception is that simply encrypting disks satisfies compliance. Disk encryption protects data at rest but does not prevent privileged users from viewing plaintext data if keys are available to the server. Another misconception is treating governance as a one-time task; classification and policy enforcement require continuous review as schemas and use-cases change. To be practical, governance maps data categories to controls: classify sensitive columns, enable auditing for access evidence, apply masking for presentation-level privacy, and use client-side encryption for data that must not be seen by database operators. Which set of controls would you choose for payment card data versus a public product catalog?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Why governance matters
Definition

Data governance and compliance

Governance ensures data is controlled and accounted for. Compliance ties these practices to laws and standards that require proof and evidence.

Regulatory drivers
GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI demand protection, access controls, and retained logs to show who did what and when.
Common mistakes
Treating masking as encryption, not reviewing audit logs, and failing to re-classify evolving data schemas.
Key Takeaway

Governance links classification, protection, and evidence to reduce risk and demonstrate compliance.

Practical mapping
If the data is financial
Classify as Highly Confidential, enable strict auditing, and consider Always Encrypted for columns such as card numbers.
If the data is public
Label as public, relax masking, but still monitor for anomalous access patterns.
Analogy
Think of classification as tags, auditing as security camera footage, masking as a blurred sign, and Always Encrypted as sealing a letter before mailing.

screens.title: Data classification and discovery (Azure SQL)
screens.narratorSegment: Data Discovery & Classification is an Azure S Q L Database feature that scans tables and recommends sensitivity labels for columns. It looks for patterns and column names that match common sensitive data types — for example, credit card formats, email addresses, names, and personal identifiers — and suggests an information type and sensitivity label like Confidential or Highly Confidential. After a scan you can accept, modify, or add classifications to better match your business context. Classification matters because it is the input for reporting, for audit workflows, and for automated policy checks. A concrete example: run a classification scan on a Sales. Customers table and the tool recommends marking CreditCardNumber as Financial and Highly Confidential, and Email as Contact Info and Confidential. A common misconception is that classification automatically applies masking or encryption. It does not — classification only tags data so other controls can be applied. Use classification reports to demonstrate coverage during an audit and to drive automation through Azure Policy. How often will you schedule scans to ensure new columns are captured? Data classification and discovery (Azure SQL) means classification is a discovery and tagging step that informs protection, auditing, and policy enforcement — it does not itself change data.. In practical terms, how data discovery & classification finds and labels sensitive columns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Data Classification
Process

Scan, Review, Apply

  1. Run Data Discovery & Classification scan to detect candidate columns based on patterns and names.
  2. Review recommendations and adjust sensitivity labels to reflect business context.
  3. Save classifications to enable reporting and policy checks across databases.
Concrete example
A scan recommends CreditCardNumber as Highly Confidential and Email as Confidential for the Sales.Customers table.
Remember: classification is metadata. It helps you decide where to mask or encrypt, but does not alter stored data by itself.
Reporting and policy
Use case
Export classification reports when preparing for an audit to show what data is labeled and why.
Mnemonic
Think: Tag first, Protect second.
Misconception check
Classification does not enforce masking or encryption automatically; you must apply those controls separately.

screens.title: Database auditing across engines
screens.narratorSegment: Auditing records database activity so you can detect suspicious events and provide evidence during an investigation. In Azure S Q L Database, auditing captures actions like login attempts, schema changes, and data access events; you can configure auditing to write logs to an Azure Storage account, Log Analytics workspace, or an Event Hub. For PostgreSQL and MySQL, auditing is typically configured at the server level using parameters or a plugin. PostgreSQL uses settings such as log_connections, log_disconnections, and log_statement to produce logs, while MySQL Flexible Server can use an audit_log plugin. Centralizing logs is important: streaming audit data to Azure Monitor Log Analytics allows you to run queries, build alerts, and retain logs per your retention policy. A typical architecture sends the raw audit stream to an Event Hub or storage for long-term retention and to Log Analytics for active monitoring. A common mistake is leaving audit logs only on the server with short retention. To be compliant, ensure logs are forwarded and retained for the period required by your regulation. How would you prioritize which events to alert on first in a new deployment?

keyIdea.text: Stream audit data to a centralized store so you can query, alert, and retain logs beyond server defaults.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Database Auditing
Architecture

Collect, centralize, analyze

Design an auditing pipeline that captures events and forwards them to a centralized analysis and retention store.
Azure SQL
Enable auditing and send logs to Storage, Log Analytics, or Event Hub based on retention and integration needs.
PostgreSQL / MySQL
Configure server logging parameters or audit plugins, then stream outputs to Log Analytics for central review.
Common mistake

Storing logs only on the server risks short retention and lost evidence. Centralize for durability and queryability.

Typical pipeline
Capture
Database emits audit events for logins, DML, DDL and permission changes.
Transport
Stream to Storage for retention, to Event Hub for downstream systems, and to Log Analytics for analysis.
Analyze
Use Log Analytics queries and alerts to detect anomalies and maintain compliance evidence.
Example prioritization: start by alerting on failed admin logins and unexpected schema changes, then expand to sensitive column access patterns.

screens.title: Auditing: example T-SQL audit specification
screens.narratorSegment: This example shows the kinds of events an audit specification can capture in Azure S Q L Database. While auditing is typically enabled and configured through the Azure Portal, PowerShell, or CLI, a database-level audit specification demonstrates what events are relevant: selects, inserts, updates, and deletes on a database are common items you may want to record. The shown sample is conceptual T-S Q L to illustrate the events; in practice use platform tooling to bind the audit to a storage destination. A concrete example: enabling select and update events on a Customers table will record who queried or changed those records so you can trace access in an investigation. A common misconception is that enabling all events without filtering is always best; high-volume systems create large logs and cost more to store and analyze, so choose events based on risk. After finishing this screen, consider which DML statements are most sensitive in your workload and should be audited first. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Auditing Example
Code walkthrough
This conceptual T-SQL shows a database audit specification capturing common DML actions. Use portal tooling to bind audits to storage destinations.
-- Conceptual example of a database audit specification
CREATE DATABASE AUDIT SPECIFICATION [Audit_Data_Access]
FOR SERVER AUDIT [SQL_Server_Audit]
ADD (SELECT ON DATABASE::[MyDatabase] BY public),
ADD (UPDATE ON DATABASE::[MyDatabase] BY public),
ADD (DELETE ON DATABASE::[MyDatabase] BY public),
ADD (INSERT ON DATABASE::[MyDatabase] BY public)
WITH (STATE = ON);
Explanation
  • Audit captures read and write operations to provide an access trail for sensitive data.
  • Bind the audit to a central destination: Storage for retention, Log Analytics for queries, Event Hub for streaming.
  • Filter to relevant actions to control volume and cost.
Concrete scenario
Audit SELECT on patient diagnosis columns so you can trace who accessed those records during an investigation.

screens.title: Dynamic Data Masking (DDM)
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic Data Masking helps reduce exposure of sensitive data by masking result sets at query time for non-privileged users. The data in the database remains unchanged; masking only alters what is displayed when a query is executed. Common masking functions include email(), which masks an email address, and partial functions that reveal only selected characters such as the last four digits of a card number. For example, mask an Email column so an analyst sees 'xxxx@xxxx. com' while an admin with UNMASK permission sees the full address. DDM is policy-based and easy to implement, making it useful when you need quick presentation-level privacy without application changes. However, it is not encryption: masked data can still be retrieved unmasked by privileged users and does not protect data at rest or from database administrators. A common mistake is relying on DDM alone for regulatory protections; for very sensitive data use Always Encrypted. After this screen, consider which analysts or roles require unmasked access and how you would grant UNMASK permission selectively. Dynamic Data Masking (DDM) means ddm masks displayed values for non-privileged users; it is a presentation control, not a substitute for encryption.. In practical terms, purpose, behavior, and concrete masking rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Dynamic Data Masking
Definition

Masking at query time

Masking alters query results for non-privileged users. The stored data stays intact.
-- Apply email mask and partial mask for credit card
ALTER TABLE Sales.Customers
ADD MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = 'email()') FOR Email;

ALTER TABLE Sales.Customers
ADD MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = 'partial(0, "XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-", 4)') FOR CreditCardNumber;

-- Grant UNMASK to allow specific roles to see unmasked data
GRANT UNMASK TO AnalystRole;
Practical notes
  • DDM is quick to deploy and useful where apps cannot be changed immediately.
  • Masking policy can be applied per column and can expose partial characters for usability.
  • Misconception: DDM is not encryption and does not prevent privileged users from seeing plaintext.
Example
An AnalystRole sees masked emails and credit cards, while an admin with UNMASK sees real values during investigations.

screens.title: Testing Dynamic Data Masking in a lab
screens.narratorSegment: Testing DDM in a controlled lab verifies that roles see the expected masked or unmasked values. The lab steps are: create a sample Customers table, insert sample rows, apply masking functions to Email and CreditCardNumber, create a non-privileged login and user, grant SELECT to that user, and then query as that user to observe masked results. Next, connect as an admin user to confirm unmasked access. The sample sequence shows how to validate masking without altering application code. A concrete example from the chapter uses a TestUser account: after granting simple SELECT permission, TestUser will see masked emails and masked credit card numbers, proving the policy works. A common mistake is forgetting to grant the UNMASK permission to those who legitimately need unmasked access; do not over-provision UNMASK because it defeats the protection. When you run this in your lab, document the steps and capture both masked and unmasked outputs as audit evidence. Testing Dynamic Data Masking in a lab means validate masking by comparing queries run as a non-privileged user and as an admin; capture both results as evidence.. In practical terms, create users, apply masks, and verify behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Testing DDM
Step-by-step
  1. Create the sample Sales.Customers table and insert rows.
  2. Apply DDM rules to Email and CreditCardNumber columns.
  3. Create login TestUser and grant SELECT on the table.
  4. Connect as TestUser and run SELECT to observe masked values.
  5. Connect as admin to confirm unmasked output.
Common mistake
Granting UNMASK too broadly defeats privacy controls; grant only to roles with a clear need.
Example SQL snippets
-- Create a non-privileged test user
CREATE LOGIN TestUser WITH PASSWORD = 'YourStrongPassword!';
CREATE USER TestUser FOR LOGIN TestUser;
GRANT SELECT ON Sales.Customers TO TestUser;

-- Test result: connect as TestUser and run:
SELECT CustomerID, Email, CreditCardNumber FROM Sales.Customers;

screens.title: Always Encrypted: client-side protection
screens.narratorSegment: Always Encrypted protects sensitive columns by encrypting values on the client before they are sent to the database, and decrypting them only on the client when retrieved. This means the database server and administrators never see plaintext, and operators cannot read the values even with administrative access. The feature uses two key types: Column Encryption Keys (CEK), which encrypt column data, and Column Master Keys (CMK), which protect the CEKs. A typical scenario is protecting patient diagnosis fields or payment card numbers where separation of duties is required. A concrete example: an application with a client-side driver holds the CMK and uses it to decrypt CEKs locally, so when querying the database the server only sees ciphertext. A common misconception is that Always Encrypted removes the need for auditing or classification; it does not. Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Always Encrypted
Definition

Client-side encryption for sensitive columns

Data is encrypted before it reaches the server; the server stores ciphertext and never holds the keys to decrypt.
Keys
Column Master Key (CMK) protects Column Encryption Key (CEK). CEK encrypts column values.
Use case
Protect PHI or payment data so DBAs cannot view plaintext even during maintenance.
Design notes
  • Plan key storage and rotation; CMKs often live in a key vault outside the database.
  • Ensure client drivers support Always Encrypted operations for encryption and decryption.
  • Combine with classification to determine which columns require this level of protection.
Misconception check
Always Encrypted protects column contents but does not replace audit trails or classification processes.

screens.title: DDM vs Always Encrypted vs TDE
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the differences between DDM, Always Encrypted, and Transparent Data Encryption helps you choose the right control for each requirement. Dynamic Data Masking provides presentation-level masking for non-privileged users; it is quick to deploy but does not protect data at rest or from privileged users. Transparent Data Encryption encrypts the database files on disk, protecting data at rest from physical theft, but the server and DBAs can see plaintext when the database is running and keys are available. Always Encrypted encrypts data on the client so the server stores only ciphertext; DBAs cannot read the data. A concrete scenario: for analytics teams who should not see full credit card numbers, use DDM to prevent casual exposure; for strict separation of duties where no server operator may view the data, use Always Encrypted. Use TDE as a baseline for disk-level protection alongside one of the other options. A common mistake is stacking only TDE and assuming DBAs cannot access sensitive columns; TDE alone is insufficient for separation of duties. After this screen, ask yourself which combination meets your compliance needs while minimizing application changes.

('John', 'Doe', 'john.doe@example.com', '123-456-7890', '1111-2222-3333-4444', '1980-01-15');
Apply DDM

You will learn why classifying sensitive columns, auditing access, and choosing the right protection — masking versus client-side encryption — are foundational for meeting rules like GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI. We'll use the built-in tools Azure provides: Data Discovery & Classification, auditing to storage or Log Analytics, Dynamic Data Masking, and Always Encrypted. I will show practical examples you can run in a lab: a sample Customers table, how to mark columns as Confidential or Highly Confidential, and how to mask and test access for a non-privileged user. You will also see how PostgreSQL and MySQL handle auditing differently and when to stream logs for centralized analysis. By the end you should be able to decide when to mask, when to encrypt on the client, and how Azure Policy and Microsoft Defender for Cloud help you enforce and monitor those choices. Think about a dataset you manage: which columns should be classified and which feature protects them best?

Over the next screens you will gain specific, verifiable skills that support secure database operations in Azure. First, you will understand why governance and compliance matter for cloud databases and how regulation shapes technical controls. Next, you will learn to run Azure's Data Discovery & Classification to find and label sensitive fields so you can apply targeted protections. You will also configure and manage auditing across Azure S Q L, PostgreSQL, and MySQL so access and changes are recorded and available for analysis. Finally, you will learn the practical use and limits of Dynamic Data Masking, and when to use client-side encryption with Always Encrypted instead. Each objective is paired with a brief mnemonic or scenario to help cement the skill: think of classification as tagging, auditing as a security camera, masking as a privacy filter, and Always Encrypted as locking the data before it leaves the client. These objectives form measurable milestones you can test in a lab environment.

These next objectives focus on operationalizing governance in Azure and avoiding common mistakes. You will learn how to use Azure Policy to enforce that auditing and classification are enabled across subscriptions, and how Microsoft Defender for Cloud surfaces security recommendations that relate to databases. We'll cover practical configuration steps for PostgreSQL and MySQL auditing parameters, and show how to stream logs into Log Analytics for centralized analysis. The final objective is hands-on: create a sample Customers table, apply classifications, add Dynamic Data Masking rules, and test results with a non-privileged user. This objective ties everything together and proves you can implement the controls and validate them. Remember, objectives are measurable: being able to demonstrate masked results for an unprivileged user and unmasked results for an admin is the evidence of correct configuration.

Data governance is the set of processes and responsibilities that ensure data is available, accurate, and secure. Compliance means meeting laws and regulations that control how personal or sensitive data is handled. In cloud databases, lack of governance can mean uncontrolled access, inconsistent protections, and failed audits — all of which create legal and business risk. For example, a retail application that stores credit card numbers without classification may expose financial data to developers, auditors, or third-party services unintentionally. Regulations such as GDPR or PCI require not only technical controls but also evidence: classification reports, audit logs, and retention policies. A common misconception is that simply encrypting disks satisfies compliance. Disk encryption protects data at rest but does not prevent privileged users from viewing plaintext data if keys are available to the server. Another misconception is treating governance as a one-time task; classification and policy enforcement require continuous review as schemas and use-cases change. To be practical, governance maps data categories to controls: classify sensitive columns, enable auditing for access evidence, apply masking for presentation-level privacy, and use client-side encryption for data that must not be seen by database operators. Which set of controls would you choose for payment card data versus a public product catalog?

Data Discovery & Classification is an Azure S Q L Database feature that scans tables and recommends sensitivity labels for columns. It looks for patterns and column names that match common sensitive data types — for example, credit card formats, email addresses, names, and personal identifiers — and suggests an information type and sensitivity label like Confidential or Highly Confidential. After a scan you can accept, modify, or add classifications to better match your business context. Classification matters because it is the input for reporting, for audit workflows, and for automated policy checks. A concrete example: run a classification scan on a Sales. Customers table and the tool recommends marking CreditCardNumber as Financial and Highly Confidential, and Email as Contact Info and Confidential. Use classification reports to demonstrate coverage during an audit and to drive automation through Azure Policy. How often will you schedule scans to ensure new columns are captured? Auditing records database activity so you can detect suspicious events and provide evidence during an investigation. In Azure S Q L Database, auditing captures actions like login attempts, schema changes, and data access events; you can configure auditing to write logs to an Azure Storage account, Log Analytics workspace, or an Event Hub. For PostgreSQL and MySQL, auditing is typically configured at the server level using parameters or a plugin. PostgreSQL uses settings such as log_connections, log_disconnections, and log_statement to produce logs, while MySQL Flexible Server can use an audit_log plugin. Centralizing logs is important: streaming audit data to Azure Monitor Log Analytics allows you to run queries, build alerts, and retain logs per your retention policy. A typical architecture sends the raw audit stream to an Event Hub or storage for long-term retention and to Log Analytics for active monitoring.
